units.text: A timeout tells you what the caller saw, not what broke. Trace the request from D N S and the edge through the load balancer, application, and database. Identify the last boundary proven healthy and the first one with evidence of failure.

Match observations across logs, metrics, and traces. Change only the boundary supported by the evidence, then repeat the same request and verify both user outcome and telemetry. A green dashboard by itself is not enough.

In this case error rates and latency rose just after an application release, while the load balancer and tasks are still running. Compare the time windows and traces before blaming network or database capacity.

Use the deployment evidence to form a testable hypothesis. If approved, restore the known-good version without simultaneously tuning the infrastructure. Verify request success, latency, and error rates afterward; an improvement makes the release hypothesis stronger.

Separate the stages of a client request: a name must resolve, a connection must establish, T L S must complete, and only then can H T T P and the application reply. Failures at different stages may feel identical to a user.

An incorrect D N S answer belongs with the resolver; a completed handshake followed by a server error belongs farther along. Read the exact error at the boundary that produced it, then use a test of that same layer to prove the fix.

Start with the expected path for an authorized connection: public routing, the subnet controls, and the instance security group. Reachability Analyzer can check configuration reachability, but it does not prove a process is listening on the instance.

If the evidence identifies a missing security-group rule, restore only the intended protocol from the approved source. Then test from that source and verify the service response. Do not broaden unrelated access or open the instance to everyone.

A private instance's internet-bound default route targets the nat gateway. In this example the gateway is public and its own subnet routes toward the internet gateway. Check both route tables rather than adding public inbound access to the instance.

Compare the actual route-table association with the documented path. After the scoped correction, retry the authorized update connection from the instance and check the result. If it still fails, inspect D N S and the relevant network controls separately.

The application should resolve the service name to the intended private interface endpoint and reach its interfaces. Verify the Region, private D N S, and endpoint security group before changing permissions.

Once the private path works, a service authorization error is a different finding. Test the exact approved operation with the workload identity. A connection timeout and an explicit access-denied response call for different fixes.

The load balancer checks a target group using its configured path, protocol, and success codes. Inspect the target reason code and test the health endpoint. An application route can work even when a mismatched health path returns the wrong code.

If the agreed health path is wrong, change only that setting and allow enough checks for targets to become healthy. Verify a real request through the load balancer; changing the matcher to accept unrelated errors would hide the problem.

Follow these as separate queries. The corporate resolver forwards the A W S private suffix to the inbound endpoint. A V P C client asking for the corporate suffix uses an associated outbound rule pointing to the corporate resolver.

Associate the corporate-suffix rule with the V P C that needs it. That fixes the outbound lookup, not an incorrect answer from the private hosted zone. Retest both names at their original sources and compare each result with its intended authority.

The client negotiates T L S with CloudFront, and CloudFront negotiates separately with an H T T P S origin. Check which leg failed. The viewer certificate must cover the public hostname; an ACM viewer certificate for CloudFront is in the Northern Virginia Region.

For the origin leg, verify the certificate's trust chain and hostname against what CloudFront sends to that origin. Change only the certificate or hostname configuration involved, then verify the actual viewer request and the origin connection.

First identify the account and assumed role that actually made the request. A successful role assumption does not prove that role can read the destination object or decrypt it. Trace the exact action and resource against the controls that apply.

Find the denial using available CloudTrail evidence and policy review. A simulation can support the diagnosis but may not model every control. Make only an approved least-privilege correction to the responsible layer, then rerun the authorized request and audit the outcome.

Confirm the authorized caller, bucket, and object first. The same access-denied symptom can come from a missing permission, an explicit deny, or a K M S decision when the object uses a customer-managed key. Identify the responsible layer rather than opening the bucket.

Adjust only the approved action, resource, and principal at the identified boundary. Then repeat the authorized read and check evidence. Keep public-access protections and other permissions unchanged unless there is a separately authorized requirement.

Follow the encrypted data key to K M S. If the request is authorized, K M S returns a plaintext data key for the authorized workload to use on the payload. A database or bucket permission alone does not grant this key use.

Verify the actual key, Region, calling role, and required encryption context. Review policy or grants for that protected workload. Test the original authorized operation again and confirm it succeeds without giving other workloads wider key access.

Begin with a trace that crosses the load balancer, application, and database. Compare request latency with connection waits, query execution, and database signals. A slow request can spend most of its time waiting for a connection rather than running S Q L.

Fix the bottleneck you measured: investigate a repeated query or index issue before increasing capacity blindly. Repeat the comparable workload and check tail latency, errors, and database health so unrelated changes cannot masquerade as a fix.

When a queue grows, compare oldest-message age and throughput with consumer errors and capacity. A failing message may retry while healthy work accumulates, but adding consumers will not fix an error that happens on every attempt.

Match the change to the cause: fix the message processing error or scale the constrained consumers. Check visibility and dead-letter settings without discarding evidence. Verify that age falls and successful processing rises.

Dynamo D B throttling can be uneven. Confirm whether the hot workload is limited by a key range, table capacity, or a secondary index. Compare table and index evidence before adding capacity to the wrong resource.

If a key is hot, spread access where the data model allows; if capacity is the limit, choose the appropriate capacity adjustment. Use bounded retry with backoff and verify decline in throttles without hiding application latency.
